summary: Defines managed objects for monitoring iSNS servers, which provide name services for iSCSI and iFCP storage on IP networks, including information on registered objects. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A directory helps storage devices find each other. This note lists what an administrator can check about that directory.

subtitle: A read-only SNMP view into an iSNS server: what is registered, how it is grouped, and when the server starts or stops.

tldr.problem: iSNS servers keep the directory that IP storage devices (iSCSI and iFCP) use to find each other, but administrators had no standard way to watch those servers over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4939 defines the ISNS-MIB module, a set of read-only tables describing each managed iSNS server, its Discovery Domains and registered objects, plus notifications for server start and shutdown.
tldr.outcome: Operators can monitor several iSNS servers through one SNMP agent. The module defines no read-write objects, so it cannot be used to change a server.

today: RFC 4939 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the iSNS MIB Is For
sections.content:
The iSNS protocol, defined in RFC 4171, lets IP-based storage devices register themselves and discover other storage devices dynamically. It can group devices into Discovery Domains, and Discovery Domains into Discovery Domain Sets.

RFC 4939 adds a MIB (Management Information Base) so that the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) can monitor iSNS servers that support iSCSI (RFC 3720) and iFCP (RFC 4172). The module is written in SMIv2, the Structure of Management Information, as part of the Internet-Standard Management Framework described in RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Storage machines look each other up in a directory. This note describes the window an administrator can look through to check on that directory.

sections.title: Objects an iSNS Server Tracks
sections.content:
The RFC starts with an entity-relationship picture of what can be registered in an iSNS server. A network entity owns portals; a portal group maps portals to storage nodes; storage nodes can belong to Discovery Domains, and Discovery Domains to Discovery Domain Sets. Fibre Channel devices map to storage nodes as well.

  • Entities are collections of storage nodes and portals.
  • Portals are logical IP address and TCP/UDP port pairs that give access to the storage nodes in an entity.
  • Portal groups map portals to the iSCSI storage nodes in an entity.
  • iSCSI nodes are individual storage targets or initiators.
  • FC ports and FC nodes belong to an iFCP gateway.
  • Discovery Domains (DD) are collections of storage nodes and portals that are allowed to discover one another.

A Discovery Domain Set (DDS) can be enabled or disabled, which enables or disables its member Discovery Domains. Domains inside an enabled DDS are the ones the iSNS server enforces.
sections.eli5: Think of a school with classrooms and clubs. Each kid (storage node) can join clubs (Discovery Domains), and a club can only see members who share a club with it. Switching a whole group of clubs on or off is like a Discovery Domain Set.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The MIB has three parts: iSNS server information, information about the objects registered in each server, and iSNS notifications. The RFC says the sections that are required to implement are the ones for iSNS server management and for notification.

The isnsServerInfo section holds isnsServerTable, indexed by isnsServerIndex, with one row for each iSNS server instance. From it a manager can read the server's current settings, including the network address and the TCP and UDP ports used for iSNSP registrations and queries. The table isnsNumObjectsTable counts the Discovery Domain Sets, Discovery Domains, entities, portals, portal groups, iSCSI nodes, and iFCP FC nodes and ports registered in each server.

Several server instances can be managed by one agent. Each has its own row in isnsServerTable, and the table lists the instances managed through the same SNMP context.
sections.eli5: The dashboard has one page for the server itself, one page listing what is registered, and one page for alerts. Even if there are several servers, they all show up on the same dashboard.

sections.title: Control Nodes, Domains and Registered Objects
sections.content:
Beyond the server table, the module has a section for each kind of information.

  • isnsControlNodeInfo shows control nodes: objects registered with the server that are allowed to manage it. They are identified by iSCSI Node Name or iFCP FC Port Name.
  • isnsDdsInfo lists each registered DDS and the Discovery Domains that belong to it.
  • isnsDdInfo lists each registered DD and its members, which can be iSCSI nodes, entity portals or iFCP nodes.
  • isnsReg covers registered storage objects, split into isnsRegEntityInfo, isnsRegPortalInfo, isnsRegPortalGroupInfo, isnsRegIscsiNodeInfo, isnsRegFcPortInfo and isnsRegFcNodeInfo.

The module also defines textual conventions that mirror RFC 4171 values. For example, bit 31 of the DDS status means "DDS Enabled", bit 31 of a Discovery Domain's features means "Boot List" (the targets in that DD provide boot capability for the member initiators), and a portal's port type is udp(1) or tcp(2). The Portal Index for a portal persists across reboots only if the portal was explicitly added to a Discovery Domain.
sections.eli5: There are separate lists for the people allowed to be in charge, for each club and group of clubs, and for every kid, door and building that has signed up. Each list can only be read.

sections.title: Start and Shutdown Notifications
sections.content:
The isnsNotification section gives SNMP notifications for iSNS server state changes. Two are defined: isnsServerStart and isnsServerShutdown.

Each carries the address type, the address, the TCP port and the UDP port of the iSNS server it concerns, using the objects isnsAddressNotificationType, isnsAddressNotification, isnsTcpPortNotification and isnsUdpPortNotification.
sections.eli5: When a server turns on or off, it sends a short message saying which server it is and where to find it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this module has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If the module is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through SNMP SET operations.

Readable objects may still be sensitive. The tables that show Discovery Domain membership, which portals and nodes sit in which domains, and which nodes could control the server reveal who is communicating and exchanging storage data. The RFC therefore says to control even GET and notification access, and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Nobody can change the phone book through this window, but peeking can still show who talks to whom. So only trusted people should be allowed to look, and the messages should be kept private.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The module uses one IANA-assigned object identifier, recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: isnsMIB is { mib-2 163 }.

It also relies on the IANA registry of iSNS parameters that was created for RFC 4171. In particular, the isnsRegEntityProtocol values used in the module are the Block Storage Protocol values that IANA assigns and documents in that registry.
sections.eli5: The module gets its own official number on the global list of management objects, and it borrows protocol names from an existing list.
